content: Electromagnetism is the branch of physics that studies the electromagnetic field, a field that exerts forces on particles possessing electric charge and is itself influenced by the presence and motion of these charged particles. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field, a phenomenon known as electromagnetic induction, which forms the basis for the operation of electrical generators, induction motors, and transformers. Similarly, a changing electric field generates a magnetic field. Due to this interdependence, electric and magnetic fields are often considered as a unified entity called the electromagnetic field. The magnetic field is responsible for the magnetic forces associated with magnets. The theoretical implications of electromagnetism were instrumental in the development of Albert Einstein's theory of special relativity in 1905. History On April 21, 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted, while preparing for a lecture, conducted an experiment that provided surprising evidence. He observed that a compass needle deflected from magnetic north when the electric current from a battery was switched on and off. This deflection convinced Ørsted that magnetic fields radiate from all sides of a wire carrying an electric current, similar to how light and heat radiate, and that there is a direct relationship between electricity and magnetism. However, at the time, Ørsted did not propose a satisfactory explanation or mathematical framework for the phenomenon. Three months later, he began more intensive investigations and published his findings, proving that an electric current produces a magnetic field as it flows through a wire. The CGS unit of magnetic induction, the oersted, is named in his honor. Ørsted's discovery spurred extensive research in electrodynamics and influenced André-Marie Ampère, who developed a mathematical framework to describe the magnetic forces between current-carrying conductors. Ørsted's work also represented a significant step toward a unified concept of energy. However, he was not the first to explore the relationship between electricity and magnetism. In 1802, Italian legal scholar Gian Domenico Romagnosi deflected a magnetic needle using electrostatic charges, interpreting his observations as evidence of a connection between electricity and magnetism. However, no galvanic current was present in his setup, and thus no true electromagnetism was involved. His findings, published in an Italian newspaper, were largely overlooked by the scientific community. The unification of electricity and magnetism, later observed by Michael Faraday, extended by James Clerk Maxwell, and partially reformulated by Oliver Heaviside, became one of the great achievements of 19th-century physics. This unification had profound implications, including the understanding of light as an electromagnetic wave. Different frequencies of oscillation correspond to various forms of electromagnetic radiation, ranging from low-frequency radio waves to intermediate-frequency visible light and high-frequency gamma rays. The Electromagnetic Force The electromagnetic force, exerted by the electromagnetic field on electrically charged particles, is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. The other fundamental forces are the strong nuclear force (which binds atomic nuclei), the weak nuclear force (responsible for certain types of radioactive decay), and the gravitational force. All other forces ultimately derive from these fundamental forces. The electromagnetic force is responsible for nearly all phenomena encountered in daily life, except for gravity. It governs interactions between atoms, including the forces experienced when pushing or pulling objects, which arise from intermolecular forces between molecules. It also underlies all chemical phenomena, which result from interactions between electron orbitals. Classical Electrodynamics In 1600, William Gilbert proposed in his work De Magnete that electricity and magnetism, while both capable of causing attraction and repulsion, were distinct effects. Mariners had observed that lightning strikes could disturb a compass needle, but the connection between lightning and electricity was not confirmed until Benjamin Franklin's experiments in 1752. In 1802, Romagnosi noticed that connecting a wire across a Voltaic pile deflected a nearby compass needle, but this effect did not gain widespread attention until Ørsted's experiment in 1820. Ørsted's work inspired Ampère to develop a mathematical theory of electromagnetism, laying the foundation for the field. An accurate theory of electromagnetism, known as classical electromagnetism, was developed by various physicists throughout the 19th century, culminating in James Clerk Maxwell's work. Maxwell unified previous developments into a single theory and discovered the electromagnetic nature of light. In classical electromagnetism, the electromagnetic field obeys Maxwell's equations, and the electromagnetic force is described by the Lorentz force law. However, classical electromagnetism is difficult to reconcile with classical mechanics but is fully compatible with special relativity. Maxwell's equations imply that the speed of light is a universal constant, dependent only on the electrical permittivity and magnetic permeability of a vacuum. This violates Galilean invariance, a cornerstone of classical mechanics. To reconcile the two theories, the existence of a luminiferous aether was hypothesized, but subsequent experiments failed to detect it. In 1905, Albert Einstein resolved this issue by introducing special relativity, which replaced classical kinematics with a new framework compatible with classical electromagnetism. Relativity also demonstrated that in moving reference frames, a magnetic field transforms into a field with an electric component and vice versa, firmly establishing the interdependence of electricity and magnetism, hence the term electromagnetism. The Photoelectric Effect In 1905, Einstein also challenged the foundations of classical electromagnetism with his theory of the photoelectric effect, for which he later won the Nobel Prize in Physics. He proposed that light could exist in discrete particle-like quantities, later called photons. This theory extended insights from Max Planck's 1900 solution to the ultraviolet catastrophe, which showed that hot objects emit electromagnetic radiation in discrete packets, leading to a finite total energy emitted as blackbody radiation. These results contradicted the classical view of light as a continuous wave. Planck's and Einstein's theories were precursors to quantum mechanics, which, when formulated in 1925, necessitated the development of a quantum theory of electromagnetism. This theory, completed in the 1940s, is known as quantum electrodynamics (QED) and is one of the most accurate theories in physics. Definition The term electrodynamics sometimes refers to the combination of electromagnetism with mechanics, addressing the effects of the electromagnetic field on the dynamic behavior of electrically charged particles. Units Electromagnetic units are part of a system of electrical units based primarily on the magnetic properties of electric currents, with the fundamental CGS unit being the abampere. The units include: Ampere (current) Coulomb (charge) Farad (capacitance) Henry (inductance) Ohm (resistance) Volt (electric potential) Watt (power) In the electromagnetic CGS system, electrical current is a fundamental quantity defined via Ampère's law, with permeability treated as a dimensionless quantity (relative permeability) equal to unity in a vacuum. Consequently, the square of the speed of light explicitly appears in some equations relating quantities in this system.
